title: The Ferryman of the Nile and the Hermit

keywords: the ferryman of the nile and the hermit
full_text:
For forty years, an ascetic hermit lived on the barren cliffs of Upper Egypt, eating wild bitter grass, never speaking to human beings, and taking immense pride in his unbroken spiritual vigil. One evening, he felt confident that no man living was closer to the heavens than he.

That night, a voice came to him in a dream: 'Go down to the river and visit Abu Dawood the ferryman, for his place in paradise is beside the prophets!'

Astounded and deeply humbled, the hermit took his staff and walked down to the banks of the Nile. He found Abu Dawood, an aged boatman with calloused hands, rowing a sturdy wooden ferry across the broad, muddy river.

For three days, the hermit watched the ferryman. From dawn until dusk, Abu Dawood rowed back and forth across the swift current, carrying poor laborers, women carrying baskets of onions, school children, and beggars, smiling at every passenger and refusing to accept coin from anyone who was destitute.

At dusk, Abu Dawood shared his simple bowl of boiled beans with the stray dogs at the landing and washed the feet of a crippled traveler.

The hermit approached him and asked: 'What secret prayers do you recite, O ferryman, that you are so highly favored by the heavens?'

Abu Dawood laughed with gentle surprise: 'I know no secret prayers, father. I only know that the river is wide and men must cross to reach their families. I row with all my strength, forgive those who speak roughly to me, rejoice when others prosper, and thank the heavens for the strength in my arms.'

The hermit wept with tears of repentance. He cast aside his pride, took an oar beside Abu Dawood, and spent the remainder of his years helping to row the ferry, discovering that true devotion is found in serving our fellow men with an open and humble heart.
moral: Daily, humble service to travelers carries more spiritual merit than forty years of proud isolation.
